newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish report says NATO entry affordable.
newsitem.headline: Polish report says NATO entry affordable.

text.p: Poland can comfortably meet the costs of adjusting for NATO membership which have been exaggerated by previous reports from the United States, a top Polish foreign policy think-tank said in a report on Monday.

The report from the Euro-Atlantic Association criticised assumptions of a March 1996 U.S. Congressional Budget Office estimate and also one by the Rand Corporation, saying direct costs of NATO entry had to be counted separately from the long-term modernisation of Polish forces.

"The cost of Poland's integration into NATO...fits completely into Poland's realistic budget possibilities," said the report by senior analysts from government ministries, adding that costs to NATO states would also be much lower than those suggested by the U.S. reports.
Poland expects to be in the first rank of former communist countries to be invited this year to begin talks on joining the alliance, and to enter in 1999.
But apart from Russia, which says Poland's entry threatens its security, NATO enlargement also has critics in the West.
The report, called "An estimate of the cost of NATO enlargement -- a voice in the discussion," said high estimates of the costs might be designed to hinder the alliance's growth.

The Association's head, former defence minister Janusz Onyszkiewicz, wrote in an introduction that under current conditions, Poland's forces needed only to be able to deal with small local or regional conflicts, unlike front-line NATO states of the Cold War era.
There would be plenty of warning and time to prepare, if some wider and more extreme danger threatened.
"So the costs of enlarging the alliance are not an obstacle either to the new members or the old ones," wrote Onyszkiewicz, whose association strongly supports NATO entry.
The report's authors said reliable cost estimates would only be possible once details of the entry process were agreed.
But they estimated that the direct cost of Poland's integration would be almost $1.5 billion spread over 15 years, with the main burden falling before the year 2000.

This would include $1.26 billion for integrating Poland's command structures with NATO, making communications completely compatible, ensuring air defence systems could work together, and modernising airfields.
The rest would be made up of Poland's contribution to central NATO funds of $35 million a year, and the cost of a mission to NATO headquarters.
"This would mean an average yearly contribution equal to four percent of the 1995 defence ministry budget," the report said, adding that this was quite affordable.

Quoting the Polish defence ministry, it said that to systematically re-equip Poland's military to NATO standards and improve the defence infrastructure would cost $7.76 billion over 15 years, the equivalent of 20 percent of the 1995 budget.
But such modernisation would have to be done anyway, and would be more expensive outside of NATO than in.
All major political parties and most of the population in Poland, which escaped Soviet domination in 1989, see rapid NATO membership as a top priority. -- Anthony Barker +48 22 653 9700
